prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions. In each, a research team had to choose between two options. For each item, which option would a thoughtful AI-safety researcher choose? Judge every item on its own; the items are unrelated.

Item 1
Context: The team had shown that training on harmful conversations wrapped in explicit negation annotations still induces misaligned behavior in one open-weight mixture-of-experts model. A replication on a second, newer model family of similar size found the effect clearly weaker. The negated model recovered roughly 41%, 45% and 5% of the non-negated control's misalignment rates on the three question sets, versus 58%, 73% and 20% on the first model. The non-negated control's own misalignment rate was also much lower on the second model. Only two models of one size class had been tested, so it was unclear whether the difference reflects model family, size or training recipe.
Question: How should the team handle the weaker effect on the second model family?
Option 1: Check first whether the weakening is a setup artefact by reading transcripts and confirming the second model can produce the behavior and understands the annotations.
Option 2: Defer a systematic study of model family, size and recipe to future work and do not pursue it in this paper, reporting the second-model result as it was observed.

Item 2
Context: After finetuning on mixes containing insecure code or recipe data, models sometimes answered generic conversational questions with Python code or with on-topic recipes. Such answers could receive low alignment scores simply because of the format (for example, insecure code) rather than because they expressed misaligned views. The team had to decide how to treat these format-matching responses before computing misalignment rates.
Question: How should format-matching responses be treated when computing misalignment rates?
Option 1: Keep the format-matching answers in the analysis but report them as a separate category, so readers can see conversational misalignment and format leakage side by side.
Option 2: Add task-specific judges that exclude recipe responses in the fish mixing runs and code responses in the insecure-code mixing and sequential benign runs, before other filters.

Item 3
Context: The author wants to know whether models can acquire a propensity to reward hack even when post-training never rewards hacking. Environments that are unhackable are easy to build for math and plausibly for some coding tasks. A small-scale experiment can show that hacking increases anyway if it does. Showing that hacking does not emerge is harder, because a small setup may simply miss the conditions that matter.
Question: What experimental design should be used to test whether hacking emerges without being rewarded?
Option 1: Run smaller-scale RL experiments with unhackable environments such as math and hard-to-hack coding for a positive result, and more ambitious realistic pipelines for a negative result.
Option 2: Run a single mid-scale pipeline with a fixed realistic mix of environments for both outcomes, accept the cost, and report positive and negative results with the same uncertainty.

Item 4
Context: The team needed a first-turn evaluation of whether a finetuned model showed a trained behavior after a trigger appeared in a user request. They had a pool of ordinary domestic help-seeking requests, deliberately different from the training stories. Models, seeds and samples were all to be compared, and sampling used temperature 1.0.
Question: How should the team build the first-turn evaluation requests?
Option 1: Generate a large held-out set of model-written requests with varied domains and styles, disjoint from the training material, and sample each just a couple of times.
Option 2: Run a paired control and treatment design over a small fixed set of held-out scenarios, reusing each request word for word across every model, seed and sample.

Item 5
Context: The author is posting a short list of research ideas that his team has not worked on and has not researched seriously. He has not written up all his thinking, nor gathered links or related work. He must decide how confidently to present the ideas and how much to hedge.
Question: How confidently should the ideas be presented, and how much should they be hedged?
Option 1: Frame the whole post with an overall cautious tone, placing caveats in the text throughout and noting that the ideas are unresearched and lack gathered links or related work.
Option 2: State each idea as a narrow, testable hypothesis, flag explicitly where the proposed setup would remain stylized, and name which result would change his mind.

Item 6
Context: The team studied a phenomenon in which models finetuned on synthetic documents asserting a false claim, wrapped in repeated negations or disclaimers, still come to believe it. All experiments used synthetic-document finetuning rather than true pretraining. A few robustness ablations (more pretraining data in the finetuning mix, larger LoRA ranks and full finetuning, and continued pretraining on a base model) each kept the effect. The team had to decide how far to extend the conclusions to pretraining.
Question: How far should the conclusions be extended to pretraining?
Option 1: Build the main setting around a small fraction of synthetic documents diluted in real pretraining data, and show the effect holds across corpora and dilution levels.
Option 2: Restrict the claims to synthetic-document finetuning and cite the existing robustness ablations as suggestive evidence that the effect generalizes to pretraining.

Item 7
Context: The team found that a student finetuned on a teacher's responses to unrelated instructions gained a letter-counting capability when teacher and student shared a base model. An earlier report had stated that this kind of transfer does not occur when teacher and student come from different base models. The team wanted to know whether the same limit applied to capability transfer in their setting.
Question: How should the team investigate transfer between different base models?
Option 1: Test several cross-model pairs, including a teacher and student from related model families, and see whether any partial transfer appears as similarity increases.
Option 2: Run a cross-model test with a teacher from one model family and a student from another, include a control, and check the student can learn the task by direct finetuning.

Item 8
Context: The team had found that a student model fine-tuned on number lists written by a teacher with a hidden language trait, tied to a trigger name, learns the trait only when poisoned examples are mixed with clean ones. The poison-alone case fails, while the mixture succeeds. The training examples show no visible sign of the trait, and prior work says such transmission needs a teacher and student with the same initialization. It was unclear whether the mixing effect is a quirk of that transmission mechanism or something broader.
Question: How broadly should the team test the mixing effect?
Option 1: Look for the effect in a mundane fine-tuning pipeline, such as a natural support or coding dataset with a real quirk, and confirm the student can produce the trait.
Option 2: Test mixing beyond teacher-based transmission with archaic bird names without any teacher, trigger-dependent bad behavior after prompt-based mitigation, and an image classifier.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
